questions.q: Why can a deployment fail even when Lesson 26's connectivity sequence shows every network check passing?
options: Because the connectivity sequence always has a bug in it
Because the actual cause can be a genuine permission gap, where the identity making the request was never granted the right to do it
Because permission problems can only happen on resources with no network connection at all
Because every deployment eventually fails regardless of configuration
questions.explain: A permission gap is outside the connectivity sequence entirely — the network, firewall, DNS, and listening port can all be fine while the identity still lacks the needed role or policy.

questions.q: What does an error like 'Access denied,' 'Forbidden,' or '403' actually indicate?
options: The DNS record for the resource doesn't exist
The request reached the resource and was actively, deliberately refused — a permission problem
The resource has hit a quota or rate limit
The request never reached the resource at all — a network problem
questions.explain: An access-denied style error means the network worked and the request got an answer — the answer was just no, which points at identity/permissions, not connectivity.

questions.q: What does an error like 'Connection timed out' or 'No route to host,' with no application response, usually indicate?
options: A confirmed RBAC role assignment error
A DNS record that resolved successfully
A confirmed IAM policy misconfiguration
A network, firewall, or listening-port problem, not a permission problem
questions.explain: No response at all, rather than an explicit refusal, points back at Lesson 26's connectivity sequence — the request never got far enough to be evaluated for permissions.

questions.q: In the worked AuthorizationFailed example, what does reading the full error text let you skip?
options: Identifying which identity made the call
Checking the resource's current role assignments
Assigning any role at all to the identity
Guessing at which permission is missing — the error names the exact denied action
questions.explain: A real Azure or AWS authorization error almost always names the exact action that was denied (like listKeys), which tells you precisely which permission is missing.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say granting Contributor on an entire subscription to fix a permission error is the wrong fix, even though it works?
options: Because Contributor roles don't actually resolve AuthorizationFailed errors
Because it grants far more access than the task required, creating its own security problem later, when a narrower role at a narrower scope would have satisfied the specific denied action
Because the narrowest role is always slower to apply than a broad one
Because subscription-level roles are always rejected by Azure
questions.explain: The right fix is the narrowest role, at the narrowest scope, that satisfies the exact action the error named — over-granting access just defers a different problem.
